title: Published Oklahoma rate, taper and productivity estimates require a 13-fold stress-area change under a steady rate-state map
abstract: We test whether source density can explain a weak relation between Oklahoma clustering duration and background rate. For a steady positive stress-step population, direct excess count equals background rate density times relaxation time times a stress-area factor. Two published sets of M2.5+ ETAS group estimates require this factor to fall by 12.71 and 13.87 across a 36.22-fold rate range. Source density alone, with fixed stress scale, stress step and area, cannot match these point estimates. We construct distinct physical populations that match all three aggregates. Two also have identical full time responses. A median-time relation gives a prospective shape test for changing area. The result is conditional: the ETAS taper may not equal the physical relaxation time, the background is a lagged model estimate, and joint uncertainty is unavailable. We do not give a statistical rejection, identify the residual driver or test a new catalog. The package includes proofs, aggregate inputs, provenance, code, figures and numerical checks.

display.caption: The published productivity changes little while rate times taper rises. The steady map requires a falling stress-area factor.
Constructed models with the same aggregate inputs predict different scaled time shapes when affected area changes.
